articles.headline: Trump orders contractors to check with White House over any congressional inquiries
keyFacts: Donald Trump issued an executive order requiring federal contractors to consult with the administration regarding inquiries received from Congress, according to the order.
The White House stated that the order protects executive privileges from congressional overreach ahead of expected investigations by Democrats in January.
Companies that fail to comply could have their federal contracts terminated and future government work suspended, the White House warned.
body: Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns, their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order signed late Friday is the administration’s latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump’s family, particularly at the Pentagon.

It comes as White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations once Democrats take power in January.

On Monday, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, told US agencies that they must seek approval from his office and the White House’s office of legislative affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to the US representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to “blatant criminality”.

Garcia earlier this week sent letters directing members of Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as “protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach”, arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government”.

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.
Friday’s executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

articles.headline: Unannounced Nioh 3 Complete Edition has been rated in Korea
keyFacts: South Korea's game rating board has rated an unannounced Nioh 3 Complete Edition, according to a listing spotted by Insider Gaming.
The GRAC listing describes the game as a compilation of additional content for the dark Sengoku action RPG and assigns it a 19+ rating for violence.
Koei Tecmo has not yet officially announced the Complete Edition, and Eurogamer has contacted the publisher for comment.
body: A rating for the unannounced Nioh 3 Complete Edition has popped up on Korea's Game Rating and Administration Committee (GRAC).

As Insider Gaming spotted, the board gave Nioh 3 Complete Edition a 19+ rating on 17th November after it was submitted on 2nd November, even though Koei Tecmo hasn't announced a Complete Edition for the game yet.

The listing, translated by machine, describes it as "a compilation of additional content from the dark Sengoku action RPG Nioh 3", and gives the rating for "excessive expression of violence", noting that "red blood and body amputation frequently occur during combat".
The listing also notes an overseas rating, which Insider Gaming says is a 17+ rating from Japan's CERO.
Unlike some rating boards, GRAC publishes its ratings as soon as they're decided, which is why game listings often surface there before they're officially announced.

If Koei Tecmo follows the same pattern as Nioh 2, there may not be long to wait. GRAC's records show Nioh 2 was rated in January 2020, and its Complete Edition followed in November that year. Nioh 3 was rated on 14th November 2025, almost exactly a year ago.

Complete Editions typically includes the base game and all of its DLC. It could even launch alongside Nioh 3's second DLC, Bloody Insurrection, which is due in February 2027. Eurogamer has contacted Koei Tecmo for comment and we'll let you know if/when they come back to us.

Back in April, an update introduced "multiple high-difficulty Battle Scrolls" (side missions), accessible from shrines, the addition of a Stone of Penance item "which increases accessory +Values and rarities in exchange for higher difficulties", and new skills given as rewards for completing the aforementioned high-level Battle Scroll missions.

Eurogamer's review of Nioh 3 called the threequel a new high for the 'masocore' series and "the crucible in which all of Team Ninja's experience has been siphoned into." It's sold over one million copies (and counting) since its 6th February launch.

articles.headline: AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it
keyFacts: On November 15, AWS confirmed an incident in its us-east-1 region that disrupted 11 services between 3:05 AM and 6:53 AM PST.
The disruption went largely unnoticed because it affected engineers signing into AWS accounts rather than consumer apps on pre-dawn Sunday.
Larger simultaneous outages at Microsoft and nationwide air traffic control also drew public attention away from the AWS incident.
body: My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?"

It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn g ot salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.

If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike.

AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds.
But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?"
Easy: it did.
Everything breaks, all the time, including the narrative

AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed.
But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1.

At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud ). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM.

Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting.
A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early.
Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working.

Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done a great job of level-setting what kind of outage was going to get attention, and "us-east-1 being weird but the apps still work" doesn't cut it.

Downdetector – which is owned by Accenture , so it's not like AWS doesn't have a throat to choke if they want to stop picking on reporters – measures consumer screaming. Originally, it was largely Twitter semantic analytics. This isn't a bad thing! As I said, I want to know if the internet is breaking. We can sort out exactly what part later.
The November 15 outage didn't produce that kind of screaming. Ironically, the tool that AWS is complaining about in the newspaper is the reason they skated by without notice on this outage.
Counterintuitively, Downdetector reports that outages have decreased since about 2022. Instead, what we're seeing is large-scale centralization.

Our companies don't run email systems internally anymore; we outsource to large technology companies who are almost universally better at fixing and resolving large-scale issues than we will be internally. And it feels unkind to dunk on those hard-working folks for their outages; would we want them to dunk on us for ours?
("Wait, don't you own stop.lying.cloud ?" "Do as I say, not as I do.")

But whether anyone notices depends upon what layer broke, and when. If my company's email system broke on Monday, and your company's email system broke on Tuesday, the story would stop at "computers suck." But when everyone's email system goes down at once, the world takes notice.

Microsoft had to tell the whole world about a bug it mostly sat on since July. AWS hasn't had to tell anyone anything. My editor runs a tech publication that covers this stuff for a living and didn't know. You can't buy PR like this, and AWS didn't have to.
If I were AWS, I'd stop complaining about Downdetector and send it a fruit basket. ®

articles.headline: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
keyFacts: Diplomats at the United Nations agreed to spend two years discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, negotiators announced.
The ICRC and the United Nations secretary-general urged legally binding rules within a year to prevent machines from making killing decisions.
Under the compromise, autonomous weapons will remain unregulated for at least two years while nations propose binding or optional rules.
body: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan, 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.

Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
Algorithms making life-and-death decisions

"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."

No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
A "nothing burger"

The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.

"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.

"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."

But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

articles.headline: Is Raphael Warnock running for president?
keyFacts: Sen. Raphael Warnock stated he is keeping options open regarding a potential 2028 Democratic presidential bid.
Warnock explained that Democrats can win in the South by visiting rural communities and building multiracial coalitions around shared concerns.
Warnock emphasized that resolving tough international issues like the Israeli-Palestinian conflict requires strong American presidential leadership.
body: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA) has kept the door open on a presidential bid. | Finn Gomez/Getty Images

The 2026 midterm elections were less than three weeks ago — and the new Democratic congressional majorities chosen by voters are still more than a month from taking office — but if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary isn’t fully underway, then at the very least, potential candidates are already starting to jockey for position.

Some of that maneuvering was on display earlier this month at the fittingly named “What’s Next” political conference in Denver. The conference drew Democratic operatives, strategists, and presidential hopefuls from around the country — and Vox’s America, Actually podcast, where host Astead Herndon asked attendees for their thoughts about Democratic Party’s future.

Herndon also sat down with one possible 2028 candidate: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA). His background is especially relevant after the midterms: He’s the senior pastor at the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta at a time when more Democratic candidates are embracing religious appeals ; and he’s a student of the civil rights movement, the legacy of which could be seen in surging Black turnout across the South after the Supreme Court rolled back parts of the Voting Rights Act.
Warnock has kept the door open on a presidential bid ; his colleague Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) is also frequently discussed as a potential candidate .

Herndon and Warnock discussed how Democrats can win in the South following election victories by Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom and others; why Warnock made the trip to Michigan to campaign for Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed; and the need for presidential leadership to resolve some of America’s toughest problems at home and abroad.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel .
I feel like some of the reason the South hasn’t seen some of that investment is a presumption that white Southerners are unpersuadable.

And in your race, and I think what happened in Georgia, it wasn’t just turnout, but it was also persuasion. It was convincing people to move on from Republicans and embrace Democrats. How do you make that persuasion happen?

As a pastor, there’s something that I call the ministry of presence. Sometimes you can’t solve people’s problems because they’re complicated or complex. They may take time, or you may not be able to fix it immediately. But there’s something healing about having people show up for you.

And so when I was running in 2021, and then again had to turn around and run in 2022, I would show up in these little towns all across Georgia. The folks were surprised that I was there. And you might be thinking, “Well, of course they were surprised that a Democrat was there.” No, they were surprised that anybody running for the United States Senate was in their little town.

And as we sat down and talked about their hospital that had just closed, as we talked about the struggles that their farmers were having under the tariffs that Trump imposed in his first term, we realized that we had things in common, and we shared a faith. And I got enough of those voters to build the kind of moral, multiracial coalition to win.
Some of the playbook here, though, feels kind of intuitive. You know, show up, lean in to a kind of shared identity. Campaign everywhere.

Even when I’ve heard Southerners talk about building structures over a long period of time, part of me wonders: Why has it been such an effort to make that happen? Are we talking around racism here? Is it just because these are people who have been written off?

That’s a good point, and it’s an interesting thing. Here’s what Black Southerners and white Southerners have in common — particularly poor white Southerners in these rural districts: They’re written off. Like, that’s a shared identity. And if we’re ever to have a moment in this country that transforms it into something that Dr. King called the beloved community, we’ll somehow traverse those boundaries and recognize how much we have in common and how much our interests are connected.

I thought it was really interesting how you went to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, who obviously was victorious in that race. You made a clear pitch to Black voters. I thought it was an interesting message. I want you to just describe it — why was that advocacy important to you?

First of all, I wanted us to win the majority. But also, as I looked at that debate as it was unfolding, I had to show up. I’m a child of the Black church. And when we say the Black church, let me hasten because people don’t know this history.

We’ve never meant anything racially exclusive about that. Black church is just a moniker for the anti-slavery church. Because almost all of American Christianity acquiesced — not just acquiesced, aided and provided a kind of moral covering, if you will, for slavery. So the Black church was literally born fighting for freedom. It was born fighting bigotry.
“We need somebody who doesn’t need the job; who really is driven by a deep sense of moral vocation and mission, and for whom the job is a set of tools.”

And when I saw the all-out assault on Brother Abdul on the basis of his religious identity — bigotry is bigotry, and religious bigotry is bigotry. The Black church was born fighting bigotry. And so you literally have people saying that he’s unfit because of where he prays and how he prays.
And if there was anybody that I felt should be the tip of the spear rejecting that idea, it was the Black church, and so I went, among other things, to remind my colleagues there of who we are.

It wasn’t just Republicans who used some of those Islamophobic attacks. There was the infamous scene of Haley Stevens , the Democratic congresswoman who lost that primary, going to the Black church [with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers].
Here she is standing with somebody who is engaged in this kind of Islamophobic rhetoric, and she’s in a Black church doing this. It’s deeply insulting.

We had Abdul El-Sayed on our show , and he made the case for cutting off aid to Israel. In 2025, you and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff voted to block a measure from Bernie Sanders that would’ve stopped $8 billion in aid for Israel.
I recently saw a stat that 74 percent of Democrats oppose additional funding for Israel, per a poll from the New York Times and Siena . Was that vote a mistake?
We’ve had several [Joint Resolution of Disapproval] votes. You chose only to mention the one that I didn’t vote for. I have voted on multiple occasions to limit military aid to Israel.

My North Star where that issue is concerned is a region where Israeli mothers and Palestinian mothers can put their children to sleep at night, know that they’re safe, and have them awaken to a world that embraces their full humanity.

I support a two-state solution. Clearly, Netanyahu does not. He is a problem. and what we need in this moment is leadership. I don’t shirk that one bit. But I will tell you this, as someone who has voted for these [joint resolutions] on a few occasions in response to the moral atrocities that we’ve seen in Gaza, I can tell you that what I’ve learned is that there is no replacement for presidential leadership, and we haven’t had that on this issue in quite some time.
Would you include President Biden in that?
We have not had the kind of leadership that I would want to see on that issue in quite some time. The people are crying out for more.
I am just old enough to remember when an American president took two old men in a room at Camp David and he wouldn’t let them go until they worked something out.

Of course, Anwar Sadat paid a very high price for that. I remember that, too. I think I was in seventh grade. We need American presidential leadership in this moment for that and for a whole range of reasons.
You’ve mentioned presidential leadership. What’s one nonnegotiable for the next Democratic presidential nominee? What’s one thing you think they have to do?

We need somebody who doesn’t need the job; who really is driven by a deep sense of moral vocation and mission, and for whom the job is a set of tools. But the mission is what is central. I think when you have somebody who’s grounded in that kind of deep commitment, then we’re onto something.

I’ve seen you kind of dodge this question about whether you’re considering a run for president in 2028. Your go-to answer was, “Well, I’m focused on the midterms.” Now that we have results from the midterms, I’m going ask you again.
Are you thinking about running for president in 2028?
I remain very committed, and deeply honored to be in this fight for the people of Georgia.
You know, who gets to represent 11 million people? Stand up, get up, fight for them every day? And I remain prayerful about what’s the best use of my gifts in this moment.
I hope that at the end of my life, I will have poured it all out and gone ’till the wheels fall off. And that’s what I’m trying to do — give it all I have.
Give me a sense of how that decision calculus works. Very few people are ever in the position to think about such a thing. How do you go about making a decision about whether that’s true for you?
I have been praying this prayer since I was a kid. I ask God to order my steps. And so you just do the work, and I think you’ll know what you need to do when the time comes.

articles.headline: “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
keyFacts: US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs during the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos.
Racial views of human nature are re-emerging in Western politics, fuelling far-right propaganda and misinformation strategies on social media.
A network of people produces methodologically flawed work claiming to show innate differences among racial groups and manages to publish it in some mainstream academic journals.
body: At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

What got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality, or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.

This group produces work that has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research. Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.
How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?

articles.headline: New Hyundai Elantra Hybrid Debuts With 53 Mpg, AI in the Dash
keyFacts: Hyundai revealed the 2027 Elantra sedan and 2028 Elantra Hybrid at the LA Auto Show with a targeted 53 mpg for the hybrid.
The new models feature the Gleo AI voice assistant, an Android Automotive OS-based dashboard, and a larger exterior design.
Hyundai announced that the 2027 Elantra sedan is expected to arrive in early 2027, followed by the hybrid in late 2027.
body: Hyundai pulled back the cover on the new 2027 Elantra sedan and 2028 Elantra Hybrid this week at the LA Auto Show, and, wow, it looks like nothing else in its class. The bold styling may not be for everyone — though, personally, I dig it — but economy car shoppers will certainly be interested in the compact hybrid sedan’s targeted 53 mpg and Gleo, Hyundai’s new AI voice assistant that controls the automaker’s new Android Automotive OS-based dashboard tech.

The humble Hyundai Elantra hasn’t historically been a sexy car, but it remains an important one for the brand. It’s the automaker’s second-bestselling vehicle, behind only the Tucson. More importantly, the Elantra is one of the stalwarts of the affordable compact sedan class, a segment that many US automakers have abandoned in favor of more profitable SUVs. At a time when buyers are more sensitive than ever to inflated fuel costs and sticker prices, economy car options like the Elantra and its second-generation hybrid powertrain are worth our attention.
More powerful and efficient hybrid

The updated hybrid powertrain pairs a 1.6-liter four-cylinder gasoline engine with a 6-speed dual-clutch automatic gearbox. Combined output at the front wheels rises to 155 horsepower (up from 139 hp in the current car), thanks to a more powerful 45-kilowatt electric-assist motor (up from 32kW).
More from CNET

An updated regenerative braking system recaptures energy when slowing and now offers an “EV-like one-pedal driving experience” that can bring the car to a complete stop at its maximum setting. Additionally, the hybrid now features a new Stay mode that lets the climate control and infotainment systems run while parked for up to 30 minutes without firing up the gas engine.

Sharing the stage in LA, the new nonhybrid Elantra arrives with the same 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine and continuously variable transmission as the current generation. At 147 hp with a target of 35 mpg combined, it’s no more powerful than before, but it should also be no less efficient, despite the sedan’s increased size. I’d say the hybrid is the better choice, though it will likely also be the more expensive powertrain option.
Pleos Connect, Gleo AI

Inside, a new cockpit design moves the now-hoodless digital instrument cluster, a 9.9-inch “Slim Information Display,” away from the driver and toward the windshield on the dashboard. The new placement, similar to what I’ve seen on recent Toyota models, puts vehicle information closer to the driver’s line of sight.

Pleos Connect, Hyundai’s new Android Automotive OS-based infotainment suite, lives on a 12.9-inch center display. Despite being based on Android, it still features the automaker’s bespoke navigation and media software, rather than Google Maps. The system is said to be over-the-air updatable and features standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto for drivers who’d rather bring their own apps on the road.

The Pleos dashboard OS is matched with Gleo AI (who names these things?!), which is Hyundai’s new AI voice assistant that lets drivers and passengers talk to the car rather than occupy a hand on the touchscreen. Hyundai says the system features “contextual language support, multi-command capability and zone-specific recognition,” which basically means the car knows who’s talking to it and which seat they’re in and can assign context to voice prompts based on the situation.
Anything but anonymous

“Affordable doesn’t have to be anonymous,” said Olabisi Boyle, Hyundai’s senior vice president of product, at the unveiling. I agree: Hyundai’s designers clearly aren’t afraid to push the design envelope, and the new Elantra is anything but bland.

The sedan introduces the automaker’s Art of Steel design language, with chunky flared fenders that feel inspired by the brand’s recent new SUVs. The tall greenhouse looks a bit cartoonish if you catch it at the wrong angle, but it provides increased headroom inside. From certain angles, the sedan’s beefy fenders remind me of an angular Korean take on the Subaru WRX. From other viewpoints, I can see inspiration from Hyundai’s N Vision 74 concept and the hydrogen-fueled Nexo, particularly in the triangular rear windows.

The sedan measures 188.8 inches bumper-to-bumper on a 108.3-inch wheelbase that is 1.2 inches longer than the current model’s. Hyundai says the stretch for this generation improves rear-passenger space, now rated at 39.1 inches of legroom on the second row. The Elantra, according to its designers, now approaches the interior volume of a midsize car, a claim I’d take with a grain of salt had I not watched multiple six-foot-plus attendees slip into the back seat with relative ease.
Arriving next year

Hyundai did not announce pricing or detailed specs at the auto show debut, and availability is still vague. However, based on the stated model years, which are usually slightly offset from calendar years, I expect the 2027 Elantra sedan to arrive in early 2027, with the 2028 Elantra Hybrid following in late 2027.
Editors’ note: Antuan Goodwin’s travel costs were covered by Genesis. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

articles.headline: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to kill Ukrainian American rapper on its soil
keyFacts: Danish authorities thwarted an alleged Russian intelligence plot to assassinate Ukrainian American rapper Kyivstoner, the Danish prime minister's office said.
Police arrested two Danish gang members carrying weapons before the concert, and Denmark expelled a Russian defense attaché, officials stated.
The Russian embassy said the accusations lacked proof, while European Union leaders expressed solidarity with Denmark.
body: COPENHAGEN, Denmark — Authorities thwarted the attempted killing of a Ukrainian American citizen on Danish soil in a plot allegedly orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, the Danish prime minister’s office said Friday.

The Russian defense attaché has been expelled from Denmark in response, Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. Two alleged members of the outlawed Danish gang “Loyal to Familia” have been arrested in connection with the attempted killing, police said.
Danish broadcaster DR, citing a court hearing, reported the men are suspected of having been recruited to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper ahead of a planned performance.
Police thwarted the alleged plot when they arrested the two men shortly before the rapper Kyivstoner’s September 25 concert, which was later cancelled.

It was unclear how police identified the two men, who were stopped in a vehicle carrying several weapons, or how the investigation expanded to include two other men who are not accused of participating in the alleged assassination plot targeting Kyivstoner.
However, all four men have been held in custody since September, according to the broadcaster.
It was also unclear how the Russian intelligence services allegedly recruited the two Danish suspects.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said: “It is a clear illustration of the grave security situation Denmark and Europe find ourselves in. We are facing a Russia under pressure which is acting more aggressively and is more willing to take risks.”

The Danes’ announcement came as tensions between Europe and Russia heightened again Friday. Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Saturday the E.U. stands in full solidarity with Denmark.
“This was an attack on E.U. soil. And it is unacceptable. We stand in full solidarity with Denmark. And with all Member States targeted by Russian hybrid attacks,” she said in an X post.
European Council President António Costa said: “We will not be intimidated. Russia’s tactics and threats will not weaken the European Union’s resolve to continue supporting Ukraine.”
The Russian embassy in Copenhagen said on Friday the accusations were not backed with proof.

articles.headline: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
keyFacts: BBC tests of four major AI chatbots for Black Friday deals found mixed results, including broken retailer links and inaccurate prices.
Consumer group Which? warned that inaccurate chatbot pricing wastes time for Black Friday shoppers trying to find budget deals.
Business advisor Naureen Mohammed said she suspects advertising models will start influencing future chatbot shopping recommendations.
body: - Published
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
ChatGPT - full price and not available to buy
OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for Â£499 down from Â£649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from Â£379 to Â£814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at Â£649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, Â£150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a Â£1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".
Claude - honest, but not too helpful
Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.
Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.
It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.
But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.
Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.
Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.
It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".
We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.
Gemini - a familiar pattern
Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.
Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.
The prices for one TCL TV were correct at Â£649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.
It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for Â£539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was Â£60 more expensive.
Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.
Alexa - accurate but limited
Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at Â£532 to a Â£699 Samsung.
But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at Â£616 (down from Â£749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.
Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.

All the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.
Inconsistent pricing
There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.
Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.
Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.
The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide, external in November 2025.
A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.
He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.
Will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he said.
He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".
Slim pickings
While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.
Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.
If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".
"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.
Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.
Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".
But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under Â£400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.
"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."
